summary: Describes basic and advanced multimedia conferencing scenarios involving voice, video and text. They help define and evaluate the protocols developed in the centralized conferencing XCON working group. It is an informational document.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 4597 lists the situations a group calling system has to handle, from a simple meeting people dial into to a coach listening in on a call centre. Each situation says what the conference server has to do and what the participants' phones have to be able to do.

subtitle: A catalogue of group call situations, from simple dial-in meetings to sidebars, coaching and moderated chat, used to shape conferencing protocols.

tldr.problem: A conferencing protocol has to work in many different situations, from a two-person call turned into a conference to a supervised training session, and it is hard to tell in advance which features a given situation needs.
tldr.mechanism: The document describes basic scenarios that need nothing special from the participants, advanced scenarios that assume conference-aware clients, and a set of media control scenarios covering video layouts, sidebars, text chat and announcements.
tldr.outcome: It is an Informational catalogue, not a protocol. It is written to help the centralized conferencing working group define and evaluate its requirements, and it is deliberately not tied to SIP.

today: RFC 4597 is an Informational document from July 2006 and has not been obsoleted or updated. It is a catalogue of conferencing situations written to help the centralised conferencing working group define and evaluate its protocols, and it is not specific to SIP even though it uses some of that framework's vocabulary.

sections.title: What a Conferencing System Is
sections.content:
The document describes multimedia conferencing scenarios, and it is intended to help with the definition and evaluation of the requirements for the centralised conferencing working group. It uses some definitions and conventions from the SIP Conferencing Framework, but the scenarios are not specific to SIP. The advanced scenarios assume that the user agents support the set of protocols identified in the framework and data model for centralised conferencing, so that they can take advantage of the conference functionality. Many of these features can be implemented today using an interactive voice response system or a web interface to control the conferencing application.

The entities making up a conferencing system are the conference, which is the centre point for signalling, and the participants. The participant who initiated the conference is called the initiating participant.

The scenarios demonstrate different conferencing services. These services can be offered in a multimedia environment that benefits from some support in the user agents, which makes the services more robust and easier to use. It is up to the manufacturers of conferencing systems and the service provider to decide which services can be built and which are offered to users. The scenarios describe multimedia examples, but they apply to audio-only conferences as well as to audio and video conferences. A multimedia conference may include any combination of media types such as audio, video, text, interactive text or presentation graphics; the scenarios are similar, but the media handling may depend on the media type.
sections.plainLanguage: A conferencing system has a server that handles the signalling for a call, and the people taking part. The document works through the situations that server has to cope with, and what each one needs from the phones and software of the participants.

sections.title: Basic Scenarios That Need No Special Client
sections.content:
The basic scenarios let a participant who has no conference-aware software create, join and take part in a conference. The participant may use out-of-band signalling to take part, but that is not mandatory, and the conferencing system has all the functionality it needs to supply the service. The typical minimum requirement is that the participant supports dual-tone multi-frequency tones or can give voice responses to an interactive voice response system.

In an ad hoc conference, a participant has a service that lets him start a conference when he calls the conferencing system. He may be identified by the request destination, by an authenticated identity, or by an interactive voice response system using tones. The conference is created automatically with predefined functionality. The participant tells the other participants how to call in, by external means such as an instant message or email. The conference may be created by the first person to call that URI, or only after the owner is authenticated, in which case other participants who call first get an announcement and are placed on hold.

The second basic scenario extends a point-to-point call to a multipoint call. The initiating participant is in a call with another participant and wants to add a third. He has no conferencing functionality on his own user agent, the other participant has none either, and they do not support call transfer. He has a conferencing service of the kind described above, so he tells the other participant the conference information during the call, and both of them disconnect and call the conferencing system. The system may support dial-out, for example by tones, letting the initiating participant call the third party through it.

In a reserved conference the reservation is made out of band, in advance of the conference time. The conference identification, which may be a URI or a phone number with a pin number, is allocated by the reservation system and sent to all participants by email or instant message. The participants join using that identification, which must be routable so a conference with free resources can be allocated at the time it actually runs, and the conferencing system may also dial out to the participants. The participants may not know they are in a conference at all, since their user agent is not conference-aware, though they may learn from an announcement from the system that they are in a conference and who else is in it.
sections.plainLanguage: The basic cases need nothing from the participant's phone beyond the ability to press keys or speak. People dial a number, get put in a meeting, and are told who else is there. The harder part is joining an existing meeting or turning a two-person call into a group one, which in the basic case means both parties hang up and call in again.

sections.title: Advanced Scenarios and the Features They Need
sections.content:
The advanced scenarios assume user agents that support at least a call transfer service and a way to communicate information about events from the conferencing system to the user agent. The system may be able to discover the capabilities of the participants, for example whether they support call transfer. An advanced conference can be initiated only by a user agent with advanced features, but some user agents in the conference may have less functionality.

In the advanced version of extending a point-to-point call to a multipoint call, the initiating participant can start a multipoint call on a conferencing bridge he knows. The extension can be without consultation, in which case the participant moves the point-to-point call to the conferencing system and adds the third party, or with consultation, in which case he puts the current party on hold, calls the third party, asks him to join, and then transfers everyone to the conferencing system. A conference may mix conference-aware and conference-unaware participants, where the unaware ones may use a proxy function, such as an interactive voice response system or a web page interface, to provide some of the advanced functionality. A conference may have privilege levels associated with it or with individual participants, with privileges for the initiating participant and for regular participants, and the initiating participant may delegate privileges to others.

The advanced conference features listed are examples rather than a requirement list. A participant may add a new participant, for example by asking the system to call them, and may delete participants he can identify. During the conference a participant may switch between user agents with different capabilities while remaining in the conference, for example from a mobile phone to a desktop phone, or join by phone, discover that video streams are available, and switch to a video phone. A participant may also select different media streams from the ones he had when he joined, asking to receive an interactive text stream when he cannot follow the conversation.

A participant can authenticate another participant who wants to join, for example in a video conference by creating a sidebar between the two so the authenticating participant can talk to the newcomer and verify his identity, and can authorise participants by assigning a password to the conference or to each participant, or by approving each one directly. An authorised participant may control the presentation of media, choosing whose media is sent to each participant and muting a stream. Privileges can be given to another participant, implicitly when requested or explicitly by asking.

Side conferences, or sidebars, let a participant create a side conference with some of the main conference participants, and the participants return to the main conference when it is finished. A basic sidebar needs two participants to be able to hold two calls at once, with a point-to-point call in parallel to the main conference, and it is up to the user agent implementation whether the two streams are mixed automatically or the participants switch manually. A conferencing-system-based sidebar uses the system to create the sidebar and compose the stream mixes, which may include the main conference as an incoming stream. Mechanisms to signal the creation of the sidebar, invite participants and control the mixes should be available. Participants in an audio sidebar may not be heard by the rest of the conference, and the main conference audio may be mixed in at a lower volume or on a different channel. A sidebar may also carry a different media type from the main conference, so a video call may have an audio sidebar that the others can see but not hear, or an audio or video conference may have a text sidebar.

Further features include conference information, with participants announced when they join and optionally when they leave, and the ability to query the system for the current participants and the media streams available. A conference may have a time limit, with the system telling participants when it is approaching and allowing an extension. A participant may add or remove a media type, for example starting a data presentation during the conference. Some participants may join as audio-only, sending and receiving only part of the streams available. Some may be passive participants, listeners to all or part of the media but invisible to everyone else. A recorder can be added, recording all streams or a subset, and recorders may be turned on and off during the conference; a recorder is a case of a passive participant. A whisper is a one-way message to another participant, rendered immediately, which differs from a sidebar in that it creates no long-lived session. A participant may also ask for assistance from a human operator during the conference.
sections.plainLanguage: The advanced cases need clients that understand what the conference server is telling them, so that a call can be turned into a conference without hanging up, a newcomer can be checked before being let in, and a participant can start a private conversation with part of the group while the rest of the meeting carries on.

sections.title: Media Control Scenarios in Detail
sections.content:
During a conference, media streams may be controlled by authorised participants using either a media control protocol or a third-party application. The conference can be of any size, and larger conferences tend to be more centrally managed or structured. The mixing of media may start when the conference starts or when the initiating participant joins, in which case early participants may be put on hold and get music on hold.

For video, the participant selects one of a set of predefined presentations offered by the server, each identified by a textual description and an image showing how it appears on screen. Choosing a presentation chooses how many video streams are viewed at once and the layout on the screen. The contents of each sub-window can be defined by conference policy or controlled by authorised participants, and there may be multiple mixes per conference, possibly as many as there are participants. The typical presentations are: single view, typically showing the video of the loudest speaker; dual view, showing two streams, multiplexed either as side-by-side windows or one above the other, with or without altered aspect ratios; quadrate view, showing four streams in a 2x2 arrangement with the aspect ratios maintained; the 9 sub-picture view, showing nine streams in a 3x3 arrangement with cropping at the discretion of the mixer; the 16 sub-picture view, showing sixteen streams in a 4x4 arrangement with the aspect ratios maintained and no cropping or blanking needed; and the 5+1 sub-picture view, showing six streams with one sub-window occupying 4/9 of the screen and each of the other five occupying 1/9.

The typical video conferencing scenario is known as voice-activated video switch. Every participant hears the N loudest participants but does not hear himself, and all participants see the loudest speaker, who may see the previous loudest speaker. This mode is typical for a small conference. A participant with the right authorisation can exclude one or more participants from the audio or video mix, and an indication that they are not being seen or heard might be displayed to the affected participants, and can manipulate the gain level associated with one or more audio streams in the mix.

In the conference sidebar scenario an authorised participant creates a sidebar and selects whether it should include the media from the main conference, and the audio gain level of the main conference audio. The participant invites others, and on acceptance they start receiving the sidebar media as the creator specified. A participant who is only in the sidebar receives the sidebar media without the main conference media. A participant with the right authorisation can move another participant into the sidebar with no indication, so that participant suddenly starts receiving the sidebar media, and sidebar participants with the right authorisation can select whether to hear the main conference audio mixed with the sidebar audio. A participant can be in more than one sidebar but can only actively participate in one, and can move between the main conference and the sidebars.

The coaching scenario is a call centre or a remote training session where a supervisor monitors the conference. The supervisor is a hidden participant and is not part of the participant roster. The supervised participants might get an announcement or tone indicating that the supervisor has joined, and the other participants do not hear it. The supervisor listens to or sees the session but can only be heard or seen by the supervised participant, until becoming a normal participant, at which point the participants see the supervisor in the roster.

In the presentation and question and answer session, the conference is created as a panel and the panel participants are identified, and only their streams are mixed. After the presentation the session chair changes the conference type to normal, and streams from all participants may then be mixed. Alternatively a floor control protocol can be used, and the chair can grant the right to speak by adding the participant whose turn it is to the conference mix.

A presence-enabled ad hoc conference, sometimes described as a walkie-talkie service, is one in which a participant sends media after receiving confirmation of the other participants' availability. The participant presses a talk button, which checks the presence of the participants; if they are available a confirmation tone is played and the participant can then talk, so the media is sent to the others. These conferences tend to be long lived, hence the need for presence, and the ad hoc nature means the participant list can change at any time. Floor control can be used because the conference is usually half-duplex.

Group chat is a common text scenario in which a participant joins a chat room where the text messages are rendered in a single window and attributed to the participant who sent them. Changes in membership are often announced in the window itself, and nicknames or aliases are often chosen by participants or assigned by the system and used as handles within the room. A real-time transcription or closed captioning service can provide a similar window by converting audio into interactive text.

Interactive text uses RTP to carry text one character at a time, providing real-time interactivity, as described in RFC 4103. The session may be the main conference itself or used alongside other media types, and may represent the audio in the conference using translation services, with more than one stream where each is in a different language, used as subtitles to the audio. The translation from text to speech and back is done by transcoders, with functionality similar to transcoders between different audio or video algorithms. Participants should be able to select whether to receive text streams with the conference audio or without it.

In a moderated group chat all messages sent to the group are filtered or approved by a moderator, who may be a human or an application, and who can also remove participants and give feedback on their submissions, such as warnings before removal. Interactive text or instant messaging sidebars are perhaps the most common sidebars in conferences today, and are often separate from the conference, though making them a sidebar and part of the main conference has advantages: a conference that provides anonymity or aliases can also provide anonymous sidebars, and a text sidebar can benefit from the security, logging and recording services provided by the conferencing system. A text sidebar can also be a text-only conversation between participants who are following the main conference at the same time. Finally, the conference moderator may play announcements to all participants, prerecorded or composed before being sent, in text, audio or audio-visual form, such as a message asking everyone to come back to the main meeting from several break-out sessions.
sections.plainLanguage: This section is about who sees and hears what. The server offers a set of standard screen layouts for video, and lets an authorised participant decide which streams go into the mix. It also covers the situations where somebody joins only part of a meeting: a hidden supervisor, a private sidebar, a moderated text chat room.

sections.title: Conference Policy, Confidentiality and Privacy
sections.content:
Conferences generally have authorisation rules about who may or may not join, and what type of media may or may not be used. This information, sometimes called the conference policy or common conference information, is used by the conferencing system to admit or deny participation. For the policy to be implemented, the system has to be able to authenticate potential participants. The methods used depend on the signalling protocols the conference uses, and can include a challenge and response mechanism, certificates, a shared secret, or an asserted identity.

Conferences often require their content to be confidential. Secure authorisation of participants is incomplete if access to the media can be gained by unauthorised participants, so functions for securing the media, and for key management and distribution to authorised participants, need to be provided by the conferencing system. In some cases the functions used for participant authorisation can be used for this purpose as well.

Privacy is an important aspect of conferencing. Users may wish to join a conference without anyone knowing that they have joined, in order to listen in silently. In other applications a participant may wish to hide their identity from other participants but otherwise let them know of their presence. These functions need to be provided by the conferencing system. The conference-specific security requirements are discussed further in the XCON framework document.
sections.plainLanguage: The server decides who gets in, using the conference's own rules, and it has to check identities properly. It also has to protect the media itself, and it has to let a participant join quietly or hide who they are when the conference wants that.

items.title: Add or delete participants
items.text: A participant may add a new one, for example by asking the system to call them, and may delete participants he can identify.

items.title: Change device or media
items.text: A participant may switch between user agents with different capabilities, for example from a mobile phone to a desktop phone, and may ask for an extra media stream such as interactive text.

items.title: Authenticate and authorise
items.text: A participant can authenticate a newcomer by creating a sidebar with them, and authorise them by assigning a password or approving them directly.

items.title: Control the media mix
items.text: An authorised participant may choose whose media everyone receives, mute a stream, and adjust the gain of an audio stream.

items.title: Sidebars
items.text: A side conference may include some of the main conference, may carry a different media type, and may mix the main audio in at a lower volume or on a different channel.

items.title: Whispers and passive participants
items.text: A whisper is a one-way message rendered immediately with no long-lived session. A passive participant listens without appearing in the roster.
